title: Drill, Baby, Drill?
summary: Yes, but this time it's not Sarah Palin. In what feels like a sharp contrast to his pre‐election mantra, this week saw President Obama announce an end to the prohibition on oil and gas exploration in selected coastal areas of the United States. While claims that this expansion of domestic drilling will bring the United States closer to "energy independence" can be dismissed as political posturing, the change is a positive first step for the oil and gas industry that has been largely marginalized since the new administration took office.

children.title: Same as the Old Boss?
children.summary: In 2008, Congress allowed a decades‐old ban on offshore domestic drilling to expire. The President's announcement this week effectively served to revive an effort spearheaded by the Bush Administration following the end of the drilling moratorium.

children.title: True Impact to Come
children.summary: Exploration and development of oil and gas resources in the regions opened by Obama's announcement, contingent as they are on environmental assessments and local approvals, will likely take years to materialize. Offshore reserves are currently estimated to hold between 39 and 62 billion barrels of oil and between 168 and 294 trillion feet of natural gas.

children.title: A Step Forward
children.summary: Aside from a desire to create desperately needed jobs, Obama's belated embrace of offshore drilling is partially intended to win the support of Republicans and reluctant Democrats for broader energy legislation. A version of the energy bill passed the House last year before stalling in the Senate, where a new compromise version is expected to be considered in coming weeks.
